hints: Make the stated substitution consistently in the integrand, differential, and limits.
Differentiate $x=\cos^2\theta$ to obtain $dx$ in terms of $d\theta$.
On the relevant angular interval, use $1-\cos^2\theta=\sin^2\theta$ and choose the correct sign of the square root.
Convert both $x$-limits to angles; note that $\cos^2\theta$ decreases across this interval, so the reversal of limits absorbs the negative sign.
walkthrough:
Differentiate the substitution $x = \cos^2\theta$ with respect to $\theta$:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}\theta} = 2\cos\theta(-\sin\theta) = -2\cos\theta\sin\theta$$
$$\mathrm{d}x = -2\cos\theta\sin\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta$$

Transform the integrand using $1 - x = 1 - \cos^2\theta = \sin^2\theta$:
$$\sqrt{\dfrac{x}{1 - x}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{\sin^2\theta}} = \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}$$

Determine the new integration limits for $\theta$:
- Lower limit: when $x = \dfrac{1}{4}$, $\cos^2\theta = \dfrac{1}{4} \implies \cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{2} \implies \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$.
- Upper limit: when $x = \dfrac{3}{4}$, $\cos^2\theta = \dfrac{3}{4} \implies \cos\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \implies \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

Substitute the integrand, differential, and limits into $I$:
$$I = \int_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{\pi}{6}} \left(\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\right)(-2\cos\theta\sin\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta$$

Reverse the order of integration limits to absorb the negative sign:
$$I = \int_{\frac{1}{6}\pi}^{\frac{1}{3}\pi} 2\cos^2\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta$$

ai_rubric.Integration by Substitution: Identifies $dx=-2\cos\theta\sin\theta\,d\theta$, or equivalent; Derives integrand $\pm2\cos^2\theta$; Concludes with $I=\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3}2\cos^2\theta\,d\theta$.

hints: Begin with the transformed definite integral established in part (i).
Find an exact antiderivative in terms of $\theta$ and $\sin 2\theta$.
Apply the angular limits carefully and simplify the exact special-angle values.
walkthrough:
Apply the double angle formula $2\cos^2\theta = 1 + \cos 2\theta$ to rewrite the integrand:
$$I = \int_{\frac{1}{6}\pi}^{\frac{1}{3}\pi} (1 + \cos 2\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta$$

Integrate each term with respect to $\theta$:
$$\int (1 + \cos 2\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta = \left[ \theta + \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2\theta \right]_{\frac{1}{6}\pi}^{\frac{1}{3}\pi}$$

Evaluate at the upper limit $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$:
$$2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \implies \sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$
$$\text{Upper value} = \dfrac{\pi}{3} + \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{3} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}$$

Evaluate at the lower limit $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$:
$$2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{3} \implies \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$
$$\text{Lower value} = \dfrac{\pi}{6} + \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{6} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}$$

Subtract the lower evaluation from the upper evaluation:
$$I = \left(\dfrac{\pi}{3} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\right) - \left(\dfrac{\pi}{6} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{3} - \dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$$

ai_rubric.Trigonometric Integration: Derives an indefinite integral $a\theta+b\sin2\theta$; Derives $\theta+\frac12\sin2\theta$; Concludes with $\frac{\pi}{6}$.
